name: Nordic Social Democracy
summary: Nordic social democracy is the reformist labour-movement ideology of the social democratic parties and allied trade unions of Denmark, Norway and Sweden (and, less centrally, Finland and Iceland). Having dropped its Marxist programme, it seeks socialism through parliament and gradual reform, treating individual liberty as its central aim and a strong, benign state as the means: universal welfare benefits, redistributive taxation and full employment within a mixed economy that tolerates a large private sector. Strong unions and cross-class cooperation are part of the project.
scope: As its defining scholarship sets it out: Brandal, Bratberg and Thorsen's The Nordic Model of Social Democracy (2013) treats a 'distinct Nordic type of social democracy' carried by the Danish Social Democrats, the Swedish Social Democratic Labour Party and the Norwegian Labour Party together with most of their trade unions; Mary Hilson (nordics.info) lists the distinctive elements of its ideology after 1945 (universal welfare and redistributive taxation, a mixed economy with full employment as the main goal, a benign strong state, industrial modernity and rational planning, and a liberal concern with freedom). It is answered as a family ("family": true): the shared tenets the scholarship attributes to Nordic social democracy as such, never the programme or record of a single member party (the Swedish party's 1882 programme, Palme's wage-earner funds or active neutrality, the Norwegian or Danish parties' NATO and EU choices), and never the Nordic model's institutions in general, which the scholarship says centre-right governments and other parties also built. Its mature, post-1945 reformist position is answered; its early Marxist programmes are history. The far-left socialist parties of the region and the Third Way are excluded.

notes: Rules-5 pass by claude-opus-5-5 (2026-11-07). The first pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-21) answered 419 statements from three Wikipedia articles and the Swedish party's 1882 programme; under rules 5 Wikipedia is not evidence and one member party's programme is another subject, so every one of those answers was re-answered from the defining scholarship or nulled, with the first version kept in each statement's reviewHistory (sources s1-s4 stay listed only for that history). Answered as a family: the shared tenets the scholarship attributes to Nordic social democracy, not member parties' programmes or the Nordic countries' institutions. Themes searched: economy, government, means (Hilson, Brandal et al., nordics.info), society and liberty (Brandal et al.), world (Hilson on the EU, Koivunen et al. on the 1981 Nordic Council; neutrality and NATO are member choices, not the family's), ecology and technology (Hilson on industrial modernity; nothing on environmental policy), culture and religion (nothing found). The local corpora hold no defining text: the reference library has no book on Nordic social democracy, ParlaMint holds individual MPs' speeches (adherents, not the ideology's sources), and the Marxists archive holds only early Swedish programmes. Blocked or unreachable: SAMAK's joint declarations of the Nordic social democratic parties and unions (samak.info, Sormarka Declaration 2014 and Arlanda Declaration 2018: TLS certificate does not match the host), the Fabian Society article 'Utopia sustained' on Brandal et al. (404), the Springer/Palgrave pages for the book (bot challenge), Project MUSE's review of it (captcha), Britannica's 'people's home' and 'social democracy' entries (403). Brandal et al. is used only through the introductory chapter the publisher licenses as a preview.
